module.qc-tiling.title: Quality control (simulated QC module) and tiling
module.qc-tiling.sub: Cut the slide into patches and discard the ones that are no use
module.qc-tiling.obj.0: Explain how the variance of the Laplacian detects blur and why an artifact patch contaminates later stages.
module.qc-tiling.obj.1: Follow a pinned patch from the slide to the model decision.
module.qc-tiling.body.he.0: The model works on patches of 224×224 or 512×512 px. Before using them, the simulated QC module measures the variance of the Laplacian: a blurred patch has almost no edges and its variance drops. Folds, ink and bubbles are detected by color and texture.
module.qc-tiling.body.he.1: With the filter off, those patches reach the encoder as if they were tissue. Switch on artifacts and turn the QC module off to follow how they spread to later stages.
module.qc-tiling.body.pap.0: In cytology the typical problems are excess mucus, thick cell clumps and blur from the thickness of the smear. Empty background is the majority, so it is discarded before tiling.
module.qc-tiling.body.pap.1: A thick clump looks like a hyperchromatic cohesive group. If it passes the filter, the model may mistake it for a lesion.
module.qc-tiling.body.ihc.0: In IHC a dark fold or a stroke of ink looks like intense DAB staining. Such a patch gets a high score with no biology behind it, and QC is the first defense.
module.qc-tiling.body.ihc.1: Blur, in turn, erases the difference between membrane and cytoplasmic staining and lowers the reproducibility of the score.
module.qc-tiling.formula: Var(∇²I) = (1/n) Σx,y ( ∇²I(x,y) − μ )²Reject tissue patch if Var(∇²I) < 60∇²I: Laplacian of the intensity. Fewer edges → lower variance → out-of-focus image.

s2.note.off: QC module off: {n} tiles with artifacts pass as valid and will contaminate the UMAP (Stage 3) and the MIL (Stage 4).
s2.note.on: QC module on: {n} tiles rejected (Laplacian var. < {min} or a fold, ink or bubble pattern). They do not reach the encoder.
s2.note.idle: Switch on one or more artifacts to see how the filter detects them.

module.encoder-shift.title: Visual encoder (ViT), latent space and domain shift
module.encoder-shift.sub: Each patch becomes a vector: does it group by biology or by scanner?
module.encoder-shift.obj.0: Interpret the UMAP latent space: what it means for two patches to be close.
module.encoder-shift.obj.1: Recognize the batch effect and compare the strategies that reduce it.
module.encoder-shift.body.he.0: A Foundation Encoder (ViT) turns each patch into a vector z. UMAP projects those vectors to 3D so you can inspect them. With random weights there is no structure; with pretraining, stroma, benign epithelium, inflammation and tumor separate.
module.encoder-shift.body.he.1: The batch effect appears when three hospitals stain and scan differently. If the points group by hospital rather than by morphology, the model learned the scanner.
module.encoder-shift.body.pap.0: In Papanicolaou the stain varies a lot between laboratories: hematoxylin times, contrast of the cytoplasmic dyes and background. An unnormalized encoder tends to separate laboratories before cell types.
module.encoder-shift.body.pap.1: HSIL groups should stay together even when they come from different scanners. Compare the three strategies and color by morphology and by hospital.
module.encoder-shift.body.ihc.0: In IHC the DAB intensity depends on the antibody, the reagent lot and the scanner. A model that learns “darker brown = positive” fails at another center.
module.encoder-shift.body.ihc.1: Color normalization and SSL encoders try to make the vector depend on the morphology and location of the staining, not on the shade.
module.encoder-shift.formula: z = fθ(x) ∈ ℝ768  →  UMAP: ℝ768 → ℝ3Purity = (1/N) Σi 𝟙[ morph(kNNi) = morph(i) ]Batch effect = fraction of neighbors from the same hospital
s3.multicenterHint: The same patch with each scanner’s color profile. With Macenko or SSL on, the three converge.
s3.note.contam: Contaminant cluster: {n} patches with artifacts (QC module off) invade the latent space and lower the purity.
s3.note.random: With random weights the points have no useful structure.
s3.note.batch: The points group by hospital/scanner: high batch effect. Try Macenko or SSL.
s3.note.macenko: Macenko matches the color: the batch effect drops, but some residue remains.
s3.note.ssl: Scanner-invariant representations: the groups follow the biology.
s3.trace.excluded: Excluded by the QC module: it does not reach the encoder or the UMAP.
module.mil-attention.title: Multiple-Instance Learning (MIL)
module.mil-attention.sub: One label for the slide and 200 unlabeled instances
module.mil-attention.obj.0: Explain why Mean Pooling dilutes the signal when the lesion is small.
module.mil-attention.obj.1: Compare Mean, Max and gated attention against a distractor artifact.
module.mil-attention.body.he.0: In practice only the diagnosis of the whole slide is known. MIL treats it as a bag of patches and learns how to combine them. The aggregator decides how much each patch weighs in the prediction.
module.mil-attention.body.he.1: With Mean Pooling the positive signal is diluted among healthy patches. Max Pooling catches the signal, but any artifact with a high score fools it. Gated attention learns to look at patches with real morphology.
module.mil-attention.body.pap.0: In cytology the lesion can be 1.5% of the slide: with 200 instances that is 3 positive patches. This is the scenario where the average fails most clearly.
module.mil-attention.body.pap.1: Lower the dilution to 0.5% and check that attention still locates the signal, while the average loses it completely.
module.mil-attention.body.ihc.0: In IHC positivity covers a moderate fraction of the slide, but a dark fold or ink can score as intense DAB. It is a good case to compare Max Pooling with attention.
module.mil-attention.body.ihc.1: Switch on the distractor artifact in a negative slide: the maximum predicts positive, attention ignores it.
module.mil-attention.formula: ak = exp( w⊤[ tanh(Vhk) ⊙ σ(Uhk) ] )     / Σj exp( w⊤[ tanh(Vhj) ⊙ σ(Uhj) ] )Ŷ = Σk=1N ak sk  ,   Σk ak = 1Mean: ak = 1/N · Max: ak = 1 at argmax sk · Attention: Softmax of the gated logits.

module.xai-threshold.title: Explainability (XAI) and clinical threshold
module.xai-threshold.sub: Where does the model look, and which threshold is chosen?
module.xai-threshold.obj.0: Audit a heat map: check whether the model looks at the lesion or at an artifact.
module.xai-threshold.obj.1: Choose the threshold τ for a clinical scenario and read its effect on the ROC curve and the confusion matrix.
module.xai-threshold.body.he.0: The heat map combines the model’s attention with the biological signal. It is used to audit: does it look at the tumor gland or at a fold? The challenge compares your judgment with the model’s.
module.xai-threshold.body.he.1: The threshold τ is not a technical decision but a clinical one: it shifts the balance between false negatives and false positives.
module.xai-threshold.body.pap.0: In cervical screening a false negative is a high-grade lesion that leaves without follow-up. That is why a low threshold is accepted, with more false positives that are resolved by a confirmation test.
module.xai-threshold.body.pap.1: In the challenge the foci are tiny: it is normal for the human eye to miss them. That is where the model adds the most.
module.xai-threshold.body.ihc.0: In IHC the threshold acts as the positivity cut-off (for example HER2 3+). Moving it changes who is offered a targeted therapy.
module.xai-threshold.body.ihc.1: The heat map should coincide with regions of complete membrane staining, not with background or artifact areas.
module.xai-threshold.formula: Sens = TP / (TP + FN)  ·  Spec = TN / (TN + FP)PPV = TP / (TP + FP)  ·  NPV = TN / (TN + FN)TPR(τ) = Φ(μ − xτ)  ,   FPR(τ) = 1 − Φ(xτ)Binormal model: negatives ~ N(0,1), positives ~ N(μ,1) with AUC = Φ(μ/√2) ≈ 0.94. Φ is computed with the error function.

quiz.question: Question {i} of {n}
quiz.result.high: You have the pipeline covered from end to end.
quiz.result.mid: Good progress. Review the stages where you missed and try again.
quiz.result.low: Go through the 5 stages with the interactive controls and try again.
quiz.q1.q: Why does a WSI file store several magnification levels (5×, 10×, 20×, 40×) instead of a single image?
quiz.q1.o.0: To compress the colors and reduce the file size.
quiz.q1.o.1: Because each level is a trade-off: 5× keeps the architectural context and 40× the nuclear detail, and the full image does not fit in memory.
quiz.q1.o.2: Because the scanner repeats the capture several times to average out the noise.
quiz.q1.o.3: Because AI models only work at 5×.
quiz.q1.e: The pyramid lets you pick the magnification that fits the question: at low magnification you locate regions and see the architecture; at high magnification you assess nuclear atypia. Loading the full gigapixel base level is not feasible.
quiz.q2.q: How does an H&E biopsy differ from a conventional Papanicolaou cytology in terms of the positive signal?
quiz.q2.o.0: The biopsy always has fewer cells than the cytology smear.
quiz.q2.o.1: The cytology is stained with DAB and the biopsy with hematoxylin.
quiz.q2.o.2: In cytology the atypical cells are a tiny fraction (≈1-2%) of a scattered smear; in the biopsy the lesion covers a larger, compact area (≈10-20%).
quiz.q2.o.3: There is no difference: the signal dilution is the same in both.
quiz.q2.e: The extreme dilution of conventional cervical cytology leaves a few high-grade cells surrounded by thousands of normal ones. This shapes the choice of aggregator in MIL.
quiz.q3.q: Why is the variance of the Laplacian a useful quality-control criterion for blur, ink and folds?
quiz.q3.o.0: A blurred patch loses edges and its Laplacian variance falls below the threshold; ink and folds are caught with complementary color and texture rules.
quiz.q3.o.1: Because it measures the mean color of the patch and detects green ink.
quiz.q3.o.2: Because it counts the number of nuclei per field.
quiz.q3.o.3: Because it tells how much white background the patch contains.
quiz.q3.e: The Laplacian responds to sudden changes in intensity. An out-of-focus image is smooth, with few edges and low variance. A background patch also has low variance, which is why it is told apart by tissue coverage.
quiz.q4.q: What does the UMAP latent space of a Foundation Encoder (ViT) represent?
quiz.q4.o.0: The physical position of each patch on the slide.
quiz.q4.o.1: The diagnostic probability of each patch.
quiz.q4.o.2: The pixel coordinates assigned by the scanner.
quiz.q4.o.3: A 3D projection of the z vectors of each patch, where closeness indicates similarity learned by the encoder (ideally morphological).
quiz.q4.e: UMAP reduces the high-dimensional vectors to 3D while keeping neighborhoods. With pretraining, patches with similar morphology stay together; with random weights there is no structure.
quiz.q5.q: In the simulator, the UMAP points group by hospital and not by morphology. What does it mean and how is it corrected?
quiz.q5.o.0: It means there are few patches; it is corrected by training for more epochs.
quiz.q5.o.1: It is the batch effect (domain shift): the encoder encodes stain and scanner. It is reduced with Macenko normalization or with a scanner-invariant SSL encoder.
quiz.q5.o.2: It means the model already tells the diagnoses apart well; no correction is needed.
quiz.q5.o.3: It is corrected by raising the threshold τ.
quiz.q5.e: If the latent space separates centers, the classifier will learn color shortcuts. Macenko matches the stain across centers; SSL models learn representations that depend less on the scanner.
quiz.q6.q: Why does Mean Pooling fail in MIL when the lesion covers less than 2% of the slide?
quiz.q6.o.1: Because it only looks at the largest patch.
quiz.q6.o.2: Because it averages the scores: the few positive patches are diluted among hundreds of healthy ones and Ŷ stays below 0.50 (false negative).
quiz.q6.o.3: Because it ignores the healthy patches.
quiz.q6.e: With a_k = 1/N, the contribution of K positive patches is proportional to K/N. With K = 3 out of 200, Ŷ stays close to the score of the healthy ones.
quiz.q7.q: What advantage does Gated Attention MIL (CLAM) have over Max Pooling when there is a distractor artifact?
quiz.q7.o.0: It learns attention weights that favor real morphological features and down-weight the distractor; Max Pooling takes the maximum without discriminating and predicts a false positive.
quiz.q7.o.1: It always gives a higher probability than Max Pooling.
quiz.q7.o.2: It does not need the softmax because the weights already sum to 1.
quiz.q7.o.3: It removes the distractor before computing attention, without using weights.
quiz.q7.e: The tanh ⊙ σ gate modulates which features count. The distractor has a high score but artifact features, so it gets almost no weight after the softmax; Max Pooling only sees the value 0.92.
quiz.q8.q: In a population screening scenario, how should the clinical threshold τ be set compared with a diagnostic confirmation?
quiz.q8.o.0: High, to avoid any false positive.
quiz.q8.o.1: Always 0.50, because it is the balanced point.
quiz.q8.o.2: It does not matter: the ROC curve is the same for any τ.
quiz.q8.o.3: Low: it favors sensitivity and minimizes false negatives, accepting more false positives that a later test resolves. Confirmation uses a higher τ.
quiz.q8.e: In screening, missing a lesion costs more than repeating or confirming a case. A low τ raises sensitivity and NPV and lowers PPV. In confirmation, precision is the goal.
about.title: About
about.subtitle: Interactive course on AI in digital pathology and cytology
about.author: Andrés Felipe Cardona-Mendoza, researcher at SavIA Lab-INMUBO, Universidad El Bosque.
about.affiliation: Direction and content of the course: SavIA Lab-INMUBO, Universidad El Bosque.
about.tool: This tool was developed using Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic), under the author’s direction.
about.realHead: What is real and what is not
about.real.0: The concepts of the pipeline: image pyramid, quality control, patch encoding, MIL aggregation and decision threshold.
about.real.1: The failure types shown (artifacts, batch effect, signal dilution) are problems discussed in the field. Sources for each module are added in later phases.
about.notReal.0: The images are generated in the browser with procedural textures. There is no real tissue, patient or slide.
about.notReal.1: The numerical values (scores, probabilities, ROC curve, sizes) are simulated and do not come from a trained model.
about.notReal.2: The hospitals, scanners, cases and identifiers are fictional.
about.notReal.3: It is not for diagnosis or clinical decisions.

gloss.wsi.def: Digital image of an entire slide, stored as a pyramid of resolutions. A file typically weighs from hundreds of megabytes to several gigabytes.
gloss.pyramid.def: Set of levels of the same slide at different resolutions. Level 0 has the highest resolution; each following level is reduced by a factor.
gloss.level0.def: Highest-resolution level of the pyramid. Its downsample is 1 and its MPP is the native MPP of the image.
gloss.downsample.def: How many times a level is reduced relative to level 0 in each dimension. It need not be an integer: OpenSlide reports it as a float.
gloss.mpp.def: Real size of a pixel on the specimen, in µm. It is reported per axis (x, y) and can differ between axes. It is the reference value for the resolution of a file.
gloss.nominal-magnification.def: Declared magnification of the objective (for example 20× or 40×). It does not set the MPP by itself: that depends on the optics, the sensor and the scanner.
gloss.digital-zoom.def: Enlarging an image on screen or by interpolation. It adds no detail: the MPP of the data does not change.
gloss.optical-resolution.def: Smallest distance between two points that the optical system can still separate. It depends on wavelength and numerical aperture (Abbe and Rayleigh limits).
gloss.nyquist.def: To represent a detail of period T you need at least 2 samples per period: the MPP must be at most T/2.
gloss.aliasing.def: False pattern that appears when sampling with fewer than 2 samples per period: a fine detail is mistaken for a coarse one that does not exist.
gloss.dpi.def: Pixel density of an image in the specimen plane: 25,400 / MPP. It converts units; it does not measure quality.
gloss.field-of-view.def: Real length covered by a region: pixels times extraction MPP, per axis. A 224 px patch at 0.5 µm/px covers 112 µm.
gloss.tile.def: Rectangular block of pixels that the file stores and compresses separately. Its storage size is not the size of the patches the model uses.
gloss.patch.def: Region of the slide that is extracted and passed to the model. Its extraction size, the stored tile size and the encoder input size must be told apart.
gloss.encoder.def: Network that turns a patch into a feature vector. It takes a fixed-size input, for example 224×224 px.
gloss.embedding.def: Numeric vector that summarizes a patch. Patches that look alike to the encoder end up close in that space.
gloss.mil.def: Training with one label per slide and many unlabeled instances (patches).
gloss.qc.def: Check that discards regions with blur, folds, ink or other artifacts before the slide is analyzed.
gloss.stain.def: Coloring that gives contrast to tissue or cells (for example H&E, Papanicolaou or IHC with DAB). It varies between laboratories.
gloss.scanner.def: Device that digitizes a glass slide: it moves the specimen, captures fields with a camera and stitches them into one image.
gloss.focus-map.def: Set of points on the slide where the scanner measures focus so it can interpolate the focus height for the other fields.
gloss.stitching.def: Process that joins the captured fields into a single image. When it fails, visible seams appear.
gloss.z-plane.def: Focal plane at a given depth. Scanning several Z planes covers the thickness of the specimen and multiplies the file size.
gloss.compression.def: Reduction of the file size. Lossless keeps the exact pixels; lossy (for example JPEG) alters them. Resampling is not lossless compression.
gloss.read-region.def: OpenSlide function that reads a region: position in level 0 coordinates, reading level and size. It returns an RGBA image.
gloss.ome-tiff.def: TIFF with OME-XML metadata describing dimensions, calibration and channels. Widely used in microscopy.
gloss.dicom-wsi.def: Representation of whole-slide images in the DICOM standard, with tiles and calibration metadata inside the same object.
gloss.resize.def: Changing the pixel size of an image by interpolation or averaging. It changes the effective MPP and does not recover lost detail.
gloss.provenance.def: Label that says where a value comes from: exact calculation, synthetic image, simulation, cited source or published measurement.

m2.calib.title: Calibration: MPP and resolution
m2.calib.sub: The [[mpp]] is the real size of a pixel. It has no default: it comes from the M1 scanner profile or you type it, per axis.
m2.calib.scannerMissing: The M1 profile does not define an MPP. Type it by hand.

m2.optics.title: Optical limit versus sampling
m2.optics.caveat: Wavelength and NA are editable example parameters: the course does not state those of any real device. The formulas are ideal-optics approximations.
m2.alias.title: Aliasing: sampling with too few pixels
m2.alias.sub: A wave of fixed period is sampled with the MPP above. If the [[nyquist]] criterion is not met, the points draw a slower wave that does not exist ([[aliasing]]).
m2.alias.aria: Continuous wave and its samples in red
m2.alias.yes: aliasing: the detail is mistaken for another
m2.ill.title: MPP and nominal magnification: illustrative table
m2.ill.warn: Illustrative approximation. The relation between nominal magnification and MPP depends on the objective, the sensor and the scanner. An MPP of 0.25 µm/px is often associated with "40×", but it does not equal 40× on every device. The reliable value is the MPP stored in the file.
m2.ill.same: Your MPP ({mpp} µm/px) matches a table row ({mag}×), only as an order of magnitude.
m2.ill.nearest: Your MPP ({mpp} µm/px) is close to the {near} µm/px row ({mag}×). Do not treat it as an equivalence.
m2.nuc.title: The same nucleus at different MPP
m2.nuc.sub: A single source image with a fixed seed; each MPP is obtained by resampling that same image by area averaging. The [[resize]] below is not lossless compression.
m2.nuc.errInput: Check the values: the sampling MPP must be at least {min} µm/px and diameters and seed must be positive.
m2.nuc.aRes: Image sampled at the chosen MPP
m2.nuc.aThird: Third view of the same nucleus
m2.nuc.cap.upsampled: Sampled and enlarged back to source size: lost detail does not return
m2.nuc.cap.difference: Difference from the source (white = same, crimson = largest difference)
m2.nuc.strip: The same source data at five MPP
m2.nuc.warn: Reducing pixels does not lose a proportional share of diagnostic information: it depends on which detail matters for the task. Resampling is not lossless compression either.
m2.pyr.title: Configurable pyramid
m2.pyr.sub: Edit the downsample of each level (level 0 is 1). The level [[mpp]] is the native MPP times the [[downsample]]. OpenSlide numbers levels from 0 = highest resolution; the visual order of the list can be the opposite.
m2.pyr.note: The dimensions are approximate: the real size of each level is reported by level_dimensions. A downsample can be a decimal (for example 4.0002).
m2.reg.title: Reading a region
m2.reg.sub: The position is always in level 0 coordinates, even if you read another level. Choose what stays fixed when you change level.
m2.reg.explainFov: Fixed field of view: the region always covers the same real size; the number of pixels it takes changes at each level.
m2.reg.explainPx: Fixed digital size: the region always has the same pixels; the amount of real tissue it covers changes at each level.
m2.reg.miniAria: Slide minimap with the selected region. Click or use the arrow keys to move the region.
m2.reg.miniHint: Click or use the arrow keys to move the region.
m2.cfg.title: Patch configuration
m2.cfg.sub: Four different sizes that must not be mixed up: what you read ([[patch]]), the stored [[tile]], the [[encoder]] input and the original MPP. Each is declared separately.
m2.cfg.reduceWarn: Pixel reduction is not a percentage of diagnostic information lost.
m2.cfg.w.STRIDE_MAYOR_QUE_PARCHE: The stride is larger than the patch: there are unread gaps between windows.
m2.cfg.w.AMPLIACION_HACIA_ENCODER: The encoder receives more pixels than were read: the image is enlarged and no detail is gained.
m2.cfg.w.RESIZE_NO_ISOTROPICO: The resize is not isotropic: x and y are scaled by different factors.
m2.cfg.w.MPP_ASIMETRICO: The source pixel is not square (MPP x differs from MPP y).
m2.cfg.w.REMUESTREO_INTERMEDIO: There is an intermediate resampling between extraction and the stored tile.
m2.cfg.chainTxt: Level {l} (downsample {ds}) → read {ext} px at {ex} µm/px → tile {tile} px → resize to {enc} px → {me} µm/px at the encoder.
m2.cfg.target: Extraction size for a target MPP
m2.cfg.targetHint: Type a target MPP to compute how many pixels must be read.
m2.cfg.errLevelMissing: The current pyramid has no level {n}. Add it before importing.
m2.cfg.errDsMismatch: The downsample of level {n} in the JSON ({ds}) does not match the pyramid ({cur}). Adjust the pyramid and import again.
m2.fmt.title: File formats
m2.fmt.sub: What each format stores and what to check before trusting its calibration. Structure facts come from the OpenSlide format list and each standard documentation.
m2.fmt.svs.name: SVS
m2.fmt.svs.struct: Pyramidal tiled TIFF in a single file, with vendor-specific metadata.
m2.fmt.svs.comp: Nonstandard compression according to the OpenSlide format list; the codec is checked in each file.
m2.fmt.svs.mpp: It usually carries the MPP in its metadata; it can be missing or inexact.
m2.fmt.ndpi.name: NDPI
m2.fmt.ndpi.struct: Multi-file format with its own indexes; there is also a single-file TIFF-like variant.
m2.fmt.ndpi.comp: JPEG according to the OpenSlide formats page.
m2.fmt.ndpi.mpp: Vendor-specific metadata; check the declared MPP.
m2.fmt.mrxs.name: MRXS
m2.fmt.mrxs.struct: Multi-file format with complex proprietary metadata and indexes.
m2.fmt.mrxs.comp: Depends on the file: read it from its metadata.
m2.fmt.mrxs.mpp: Proprietary metadata; do not assume the MPP exists.
m2.fmt.tiff.name: Pyramidal tiled TIFF
m2.fmt.tiff.struct: Generic single-file TIFF with several levels stored in tiles.
m2.fmt.tiff.comp: Defined by whoever created the file.
m2.fmt.tiff.mpp: The MPP can come from resolution tags; without a clear unit it is not reliable.
m2.fmt.ometiff.name: OME-TIFF
m2.fmt.ometiff.struct: TIFF with OME-XML metadata describing dimensions, channels and physical calibration.
m2.fmt.ometiff.mpp: Physical calibration is part of the OME data model.
m2.fmt.dicom.name: DICOM WSI
m2.fmt.dicom.struct: International medical imaging standard; one slide image can be split across several files.
m2.fmt.dicom.comp: The standard allows several codecs, lossy or lossless.
m2.fmt.dicom.mpp: Calibration is part of the DICOM attributes of the object.
m2.fmt.warn: A format that does not declare the MPP, or declares it without a unit, cannot be used to compute real sizes. Check the MPP before using a file; the course never substitutes an assumed one.
m2.fmt.sNote: Uncompressed with 3 bytes per RGB pixel. Real files weigh far less because of compression, and the factor depends on the codec and the content.
m2.fail.title: Failure case: two scanners, 224 px patches
m2.fail.sub: A model was trained with 224 px patches from scanner A. In production, 224 px patches arrive from scanner B with a different [[mpp]]. The size in pixels is the same; the tissue they cover is not.
m2.fail.aC: Patch from scanner A with the field of view of B
m2.fail.capC: A read at {side} px and reduced to {px} px: field {fov} µm
m2.fail.oNuc: 9 µm nucleus in A / in B
m2.fail.oFix: Fix: read in A and reduce
m2.fail.warn: The same number of pixels does not mean the same amount of tissue. For the model to see the same scale the effective MPP must be matched, not the pixel count. The fix reduces pixels: it does not recover detail and it changes the look of the texture.
m2.code.title: Code: OpenSlide in Python (L1)
m2.code.sub: Minimal fragments using the OpenSlide API. The file path is an example. They show how to read the [[mpp]] without assuming it and how to call [[read-region]].
m2.code.inspect.note: Opens the slide, lists levels and computes the MPP of each level. If the file declares no MPP it fails on purpose.
m2.code.read.note: The values come from the region selected above. The position is in level 0 coordinates.
m2.code.patch.note: Full chain: read, compute the field of view and reduce to the encoder input. The resize changes the effective MPP.
m2.code.verified: Checked against the OpenSlide Python documentation on {date} and executed with a synthetic pyramidal TIFF.
m2.code.caveat: This code contains no clinical information. In a real file the MPP can be missing or inexact (openslide.mpp-x): check it before using it.
m2.equiv.title: Equivalent code: patch configuration
m2.equiv.sub: What you see above is this configuration. The course engine validates and exports it; you can copy it into your own scripts.
m2.equiv.invalid: The current configuration is not valid: check the red messages in the module.
quiz.m2q1.q: A model was trained with 224 px patches from scanner A (0.25 µm/px). It receives 224 px patches from scanner B (0.5 µm/px). What field of view does each patch cover?
quiz.m2q1.o.0: A and B cover 224 µm: both have 224 px.
quiz.m2q1.o.1: A covers 56 µm and B covers 112 µm.
quiz.m2q1.o.2: A covers 112 µm and B covers 56 µm.
quiz.m2q1.o.3: A and B cover 112 µm, because MPP does not affect the field of view.
quiz.m2q1.e: The field of view is the number of pixels times the MPP: 224 × 0.25 = 56 µm in A and 224 × 0.5 = 112 µm in B. In B the model sees twice as much tissue per side and nuclei take half as many pixels.
quiz.m2q1.err: Thinking that the same number of pixels is the same scale.
quiz.m2q1.app: Before mixing scanners, match the effective MPP: reading 448 px in A and reducing to 224 px gives 112 µm, as in B.
quiz.m2q2.q: You read 640 px at 0.5 µm/px and reduce them to 224 px for the encoder. What effective MPP does the encoder receive?
quiz.m2q2.o.0: 0.5 µm/px, because that is the file MPP.
quiz.m2q2.o.1: 0.25 µm/px, because the encoder uses fewer pixels.
quiz.m2q2.e: The field of view is 640 × 0.5 = 320 µm. After reducing to 224 px each pixel covers 320 / 224 ≈ 1.43 µm. The effective MPP changes with the resize even though the file still declares 0.5.
quiz.m2q2.eq: encoder MPP = FOV / E = (P · MPP) / E
quiz.m2q2.err: Using the file MPP after resizing.
quiz.m2q2.app: State the effective MPP of the encoder input together with the model and recompute it whenever the extraction size changes.
quiz.m2q3.q: You resample an image from 0.25 to 1 µm/px and enlarge it back to the original size. What happens to the fine detail?
quiz.m2q3.o.0: It does not return: enlarging interpolates, but averaging already erased details smaller than the new pixel.
quiz.m2q3.o.1: It returns in full, because resampling is lossless compression.
quiz.m2q3.o.2: It returns if a bicubic filter is used instead of a bilinear one.
quiz.m2q3.o.3: It gets sharper, because there is less noise.
quiz.m2q3.e: Area averaging merges several pixels into one and that information is stored nowhere. Enlarging only interpolates between the values that remain. The "Re-enlarged" view of the module shows it.
quiz.m2q3.eq: new MPP = source MPP · k (k = reduction factor)
quiz.m2q3.err: Believing that reducing and enlarging is reversible.
quiz.m2q3.app: Reducing and re-enlarging the inputs of a model trained at 0.25 µm/px does not turn them into 0.25 µm/px data.
quiz.m2q4.q: Is it correct to write in a report that "0.25 µm/px always equals 40×"?
quiz.m2q4.o.0: Yes: it is the definition of 40×.
quiz.m2q4.o.1: Yes, as long as the slide is H&E.
quiz.m2q4.o.2: No, unless the scanner is from a specific manufacturer.
quiz.m2q4.o.3: No: it is a common, approximate association. Nominal magnification depends on the optics and the sensor; the reliable value is the MPP stored in the file.
quiz.m2q4.e: The course presents the MPP-to-magnification relation as an illustrative table. Each scanner combines objective, intermediate optics and sensor, so the same nominal magnification can give different MPP.
quiz.m2q4.err: Assuming that nominal magnification sets the pixel size.
quiz.m2q4.app: Record the MPP (x and y) with each dataset, not the "magnification".
quiz.m2q5.q: You call read_region((x, y), 2, (w, h)) on a slide whose level 2 has downsample 16. In which coordinates does (x, y) go?
quiz.m2q5.o.3: As a fraction from 0 to 1 of width and height.
quiz.m2q5.e: According to the OpenSlide Python documentation, the location is the top left pixel in the level 0 reference frame. To read level 2 you give the corner in level 0 pixels.
quiz.m2q5.err: Passing the corner in pixels of the level being read.
quiz.m2q5.app: When walking a level with windows, multiply each corner by the level downsample before calling read_region.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.intro: Module for a 60-minute session. It assumes you know what a digitized slide is and does not require programming. The code part is optional.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.step.0: Ask for the prediction first and collect the group answers without correcting them yet (5 min).
teacher.wsi-pyramid.step.1: Nucleus section: slide the MPP and compare the resampled, re-enlarged and difference views (15 min).
teacher.wsi-pyramid.step.2: Pyramid: build levels 1, 4, 16 and 32 and a version with decimals; compare the visual order with the OpenSlide index (15 min).
teacher.wsi-pyramid.step.3: Region and patch: read the same region in fixed field of view and fixed digital size, and follow the chain to the encoder (15 min).
teacher.wsi-pyramid.step.4: Failure case and wrap-up with the M2 quiz: each student explains in one sentence why the same number of pixels is not the same scale (10 min).
teacher.wsi-pyramid.disc.0: Which value in a file would you use to decide whether two slides are comparable: magnification or MPP? Why?
teacher.wsi-pyramid.disc.1: What does a model lose when the pixels of a patch are reduced before the encoder? Does it depend on the task?
teacher.wsi-pyramid.disc.2: Why does OpenSlide ask for the position in level 0 coordinates even when another level is read?
teacher.wsi-pyramid.disc.3: How would you document the MPP of a dataset so that someone else can reproduce your extraction?
teacher.wsi-pyramid.err.0: Treating 0.25 µm/px as a universal synonym of 40×.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.err.1: Assuming the MPP in x and y is the same.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.err.2: Mixing up the stored tile size, the extraction size and the encoder input.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.err.3: Thinking that resampling is the same as lossless compression.
teacher.wsi-pyramid.assess: Suggested assessment: the five M2 questions of the quiz and a short task to configure a patch for a target MPP.

module.wsi-pyramid.title: WSI, pyramid and formats
module.wsi-pyramid.sub: How many pixels, of what real size, and in which file
module.wsi-pyramid.obj.0: Compute the real size of a pixel ([[mpp]]) and the [[field-of-view]] of a patch, per axis and without assuming defaults.
module.wsi-pyramid.obj.1: Explain why [[nominal-magnification]] does not set resolution by itself, and use the MPP stored in the file as the reference value.
module.wsi-pyramid.obj.2: Build a [[pyramid]] and tell the visual order of levels apart from the level index OpenSlide uses.
module.wsi-pyramid.obj.3: Read a region with [[read-region]] knowing which coordinates each argument uses.
module.wsi-pyramid.obj.4: Predict what happens when two scanners with different MPP feed the same model patches of the same size in pixels.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.he.0: A scanned H&E slide is an image of billions of pixels. No model loads it whole: the file stores a pyramid with the same region at several resolutions and the model reads patches from a chosen level.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.he.1: What matters for AI is not the nominal magnification but the MPP: how many microns of tissue one pixel covers. A 9 µm nucleus takes 36 px at 0.25 µm/px and 18 px at 0.5 µm/px: the same model sees different things.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.pap.0: In a conventional Papanicolaou cytology the cells lie loose over a wide area and most of it is background. The useful detail is in the nuclei and the nucleus/cytoplasm ratio.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.pap.1: With a large MPP the nucleus takes few pixels and chromatin is averaged out. The MPP decides whether the model can see what the cytotechnologist measures, so it must be known and declared.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.ihc.0: In IHC with DAB the diagnosis depends on where the chromogen is deposited (membrane or nucleus) and how intense it is. The membrane is a trace less than 1 µm thick.
module.wsi-pyramid.body.ihc.1: A high MPP erases the difference between membrane and cytoplasm, and resampling to the encoder input reduces it further. The effective MPP of each patch must be known.
module.wsi-pyramid.formula: rlevel = r0 · dFOV = P · rextractionrencoder = FOV / Er0: level 0 MPP · d: downsample · P: pixels read · E: encoder input. Everything per axis (x, y).
module.wsi-pyramid.pred.q: A 9 µm nucleus measures 36 px in diameter at 0.25 µm/px. If the same slide is scanned at 0.5 µm/px, how many pixels across is it?
module.wsi-pyramid.pred.fb: Doubling the MPP makes each pixel cover twice the length: 9 / 0.5 = 18 px across and a quarter of the area. Check it in the nucleus section.
m2.code.c.path: opens the slide; the path is an example
m2.code.c.lds: one float per level; level 0 is 1.0
m2.code.c.nompp: The slide declares no MPP: none is assumed
m2.code.c.loc: top left corner in LEVEL 0 coordinates
m2.code.c.lvl: level the pixels are read from (0 = highest resolution)
m2.code.c.size: (width, height) of the region; the returned image has that size
m2.code.c.fov: real field of view of the region
m2.code.c.resample: this is a resampling, not lossless compression
